newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW/McGraw-Hill may exit TV business.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW/McGraw-Hill may exit TV business.

text.p: McGraw-Hill Cos Inc President Harold McGraw III said he did not expect the company to buy more television stations, and he would consider swapping its four stations for a publishing or information business.

"I wouldn't be an aggressive acquirer of TV stations at this point," McGraw told Reuters in an interview. "At the kind of premiums you'd have to pay, I don't think we can justify the returns we would want for our shareholders."
Asked if it planned to stay in broadcasting, McGraw said, "The answer to that is, right now, we're very happy with the broadcasting properties."

But he said the company has "looked at many opportunities to potentially swap to some other areas that would be high-growth potential for us, consistent with other things we're doing. To date, (there's) nothing active, nothing pending."
He said the company would still consider a swap for a "more pure information business," possibly to complement one of its publishing businesses.
McGraw-Hill owns ABC affiliates in Denver, San Diego, Indianapolis and Bakersfield, Calif.
McGraw said the company would consider an alliance or partnership as a way to more broadly distribute its various specialized data, including financial information.
"We've had several chats with people more directly tied to broadcasting operations," he said. "It could take on many forms." He did not provide specifics.

McGraw-Hill businesses include financial services, such as its Standard & Poor's ratings service; educational and professional publishing, and information and media services, including Business Week magazine.
McGraw said the outlook for educational publishing was strong, as several states have pre-funded textbook spending for both elementary and high schools.
With other businesses more vulnerable to economic cycles, textbooks provides "very strong countercycle capabilities," he said.
Senior company executives said the S&P unit will post the greatest growth this year and near term.

"The biggest engine is the S&P ratings business today," said Robert Bahash, McGraw-Hill chief financial officer. "It's been tremendously powerful...They've really leveraged the franchise in many different ways."

Leo O'Neill, president and chief rating officer of S&P, reiterated that the unit remains on track to double revenues by the year 2000, and more than double the percentage of business from non-traditional products, to 25 percent, in that time. He declined to detail current annual revenues.
O'Neill said the unit has expanded strongly by getting new ratings fee business as companies in emerging markets seek to raise capital.
The more bustling markets include Russia, Eastern Europe, Asia and Latin America. O'Neill said the unit is building up non-traditional businesses such as insurance and mutual funds.
He said the funds business, which would be focused on institutional clients, should add several dozen jobs in the coming years.
McGraw-Hill's construction information group -- which includes F.W. Dodge and Sweet's Group -- is having its best performance in a dozen years, according to Robert Russell, president of the unit.
"I'm very optimistic this year," said Russell. "We will do strong double-digit profit growth, and high single-digit revenue growth." The company does not detail data on the unit.

Increasingly, more data is being delivered electronically rather than through traditional print. Russell said he expects that within the next 36 months, more than 50 percent of Sweet's revenues will be derived from the electronic side, with the same change at Dodge coming in five to seven years.
